MorphoHand · real_v1 · 2026-09-04

A Hundred Millimetres of Wrist

Every arm result in this program so far stood the UR5e on a 300 mm pedestal and bolted the palm plate straight to the tool flange. The bench is one flat table, and between the flange and the first finger joint there is a coupling, a servo bank and its wiring — about 100 mm of it. Putting both in the scene costs nothing in reach, and one number in grip.

What was not on the bench

two lines of scene, and the first arm result that describes a robot somebody owns

The chained task — grasp, lift, reorient, set into a countersink, gait — has been run on a UR5e since 2026-09-03, and that run made two geometric assumptions that were never stated because they were never variables. The robot stood on a 300 mm pedestal, so its shoulder cleared the work. And the palm plate was bolted directly to the tool flange, because the menagerie UR5e's attachment site is where a gripper goes.

Neither is the bench. The robot is bolted to the same flat table the work sits on. And between the flange and the first finger joint there is a coupling, a servo bank and its wiring: about 100 mm of hardware, still to be measured, carrying its own weight. Both are now parameters of build_real_v1_arm_scene.py (--base, --wrist-stack, --stack-density). The stack is a 40 mm cylinder at 700 kg/m³, which takes the hand from 222 g of payload to 574 g — payload the arm's controller does not model, exactly like the hand itself.

A bug the change exposed

The arm scene builder copied the design scene's world by whitelist — lights, floor, object. Building an arm scene from a countersink scene therefore dropped the countersink, and the tool stood on a bare plane while the file name said otherwise. It now copies everything except the hand.

The pedestal was free

8 spawn-jittered seeds per cell · 8 gait cycles · no wrist stack

Lowering the mount from 300 mm to the table surface changes nothing measurable. Every height solves the home pose on the same IK branch with the arm's lowest link at +0.163 m — the shoulder — and no link ever below the table. Across the whole study the differential IK reports 14 unreachable poses in 1088 rollouts, and they are all in one place: the far corner of the standing sweep, 650 mm back and 200 mm across, where 6 of 8 seeds ask for a pose the arm cannot make.

The stack is not free, and only one mode notices

wrist stack 0–150 mm, at the carry grip each mode was published with

Run the same chain with progressively more hardware between the flange and the palm, and the two ways of changing grasp come apart. The release chain — open the hand, fly the palm to the gait's pose, close on a ring — is indifferent up to 125 mm. The relay, which walks one pad at a time onto the ring and never has fewer than two on the tool, breaks at 50.

The asymmetry is the point. The release chain re-establishes its grasp from scratch on a tool the floor is holding upright, so it can absorb a wrist that arrives in the wrong place. The relay has no such moment — every pad it places is placed on a tool it is still carrying, and a placement error becomes a torque on that tool rather than a miss.

It is the weight, not the reach

the same 100 mm stack at four densities

A longer wrist is two things at once: a longer lever from the last joint to the pads, and more mass hanging off it. Setting the stack's density to zero separates them. A massless 100 mm stack runs every seed. Any mass at all breaks the relay at 500 mm of standoff.

At the highest density the release chain fails too, and the reach is identical in all four rows. What changes is the third column.

All three knobs are one knob

palm droop under the hand's own weight, at the top of a 100 mm lift

Stack length, stack mass and standing distance are three independent things to specify on a bench, and each of them moves the same quantity: how far the palm ends up from where it was commanded, once it is carrying a load the arm's controller does not know about. That number is deterministic — it does not inherit the chain's seed-to-seed chaos — and the 2026-09-03 arm study already used it as the wrist's spec, at a resolution of two points (0.97 mm chained 6/6, 1.59 mm chained 1/6).

Sweeping the carry grip at each geometry and taking the best cell it can reach collapses the three knobs onto that one axis. The order is clean, and so is the threshold.

Which makes the stack a preload problem

wrist stack × commanded carry grip, tool driven into the 45° seat · each cell is seeds out of 8, relay then release

The carry does not end in a grip. It ends with the tool cradled on the middle phalanges at about half a millimetre of interference, creeping down through the pads at roughly 1.5 mm/s, and --carry-squeeze is the one command that turns that into a hold before the transport starts. It is commanded interference: the pads are told to close past the surface, and the force that results is the difference between where they were told to go and where the plant lets them stop.

Which is why droop and grip are the same story. A longer, heavier wrist deflects more under the same command, so the same commanded interference buys less force — the arm is a spring in exactly the sense the finger servos are, one level up. The fix is to command more, and the window moves rather than closing.

wrist stack0.3 mm0.8 mm1.5 mm2.0 mm3.0 mmdroop
0 mm stack8 / 60 / 01 / 00 / 00 / 00.36
50 mm stack0 / 00 / 08 / 80 / 00 / 00.66
100 mm stack0 / 00 / 03 / 30 / 00 / 00.97
150 mm stack0 / 00 / 00 / 00 / 00 / 01.29

Every row has a window and every window is narrow: too little and the tool is delivered tilted, too much and the pads torque it out of the seat on the way down. But up to 50 mm of stack the window simply relocates — 0.3 mm becomes 1.5 mm and both modes run every seed. At 100 mm the best cell is half the seeds, and at 150 mm there is no cell at all.

Where the robot stands buys it back

the full 100 mm stack, in the seat, at three standing distances · each cell is seeds out of 8, relay then release

Standoff moves droop over the same range the stack does, and in the opposite direction. With the whole 100 mm stack fitted, moving the mount from 500 mm to 425 mm takes droop from 0.97 to 0.76 mm and takes the best cell from half the seeds to all of them. At 350 mm it needs less grip as well.

The bench specification, as it stands

One flat table, no pedestal. Mount 350–425 mm from the work. Up to about 0.76 mm of palm droop under the hand's own weight, which the 100 mm stack fits inside only at those distances. Carry grip 0.8–1.5 mm rather than the published 0.3. Everything else — the hand, the grasp, the gait set-points — unchanged.

What load it can drive

a Coulomb brake about the tool's own axis, armed once the tool is seated · the recommended geometry: 100 mm stack, 425 mm standoff, 1.5 mm carry grip

A countersink is a friction brake, not a thread: it returns μNr and no more, and the press sets N through the wedge. So the resisting torque a gaiting hand has ever worked against is whatever the geometry happened to supply — about 7 mN·m on a flat plane. --screw-torque adds a named one, as a brake that opposes whatever rotation there is and does no work when the tool is still.

The relay is flat: 14.4 deg/cycle unloaded and 14.4 at 20 mN·m, with the same seeds completing. The release chain loses the tool. Its share of the window with no pad on the tool is 49% unloaded — that is simply what releasing costs — and it climbs to 60% under load, which is a different thing: the brake acts about the tool's own axis, and a tool standing a few degrees off vertical is levered over by it during the part of every cycle when nothing is holding it.

The knob's validity, and its bench equivalent

The tool is 24 g with an axial inertia of 1.9×10-6 kg·m², so a brake much past 20 mN·m can overshoot zero inside a timestep and pump the shaft instead of stopping it. That shows up as a turn past the 1.684 gear ceiling and is flagged per rollout, and in this sweep 1 of 96 cells trip it — 20 mN·m in the release arm, i.e. at the top of the swept range, which is where the range ends rather than a clean bill for it. On the bench a cone gives no way to set this number at all — the only knobs are the press and the seat material. A calibrated one needs a brake under the receptacle: put the socket on a short shaft in a bushing with a preloaded friction washer, and the preload screw sets a direction-independent torque a wrench can read.

What this does not settle

The 100 mm is a placeholder and so is the 40 mm radius; both are geometry waiting on a caliper, and the radius in particular is only a collision proxy — nothing in this study touched the stack, so its shape has been tested only for what it weighs and how far out it puts the hand.

The chain remains chaotic at the seam, and the binary pass rate over 8 seeds is a coarse instrument: the standing sweep at the published grip is not monotone in droop, and it should not be read as one — it is a sweep of an untuned parameter across a moving window. The collapse onto droop is only clean once the grip is swept at each geometry, which is what the table above does.

Nothing here has been through the export, trajectory-clearance or servo-limit gates. The relay's Cartesian legs are a new path shape, and three of the four plans that have reached the control station failed exactly that check.

And the grip is still commanded once and never corrected. Everything above is a search for the one open-loop number that happens to fit a window whose position depends on the robot, the payload, and where it stands — which is the argument for measuring it instead. The hand already reports the quantity: grip force is commanded minus achieved, the finger servos calibrate to one spring constant across the hand, and the deflection is readable at the control rate.
